draft.title: Accuracy, precision and validity
card: Accuracy
how close a result is to the true value. A measured boiling point of 99.8 °C for pure water at sea level is very accurate.
Precision
how close repeated measurements are to each other. Results can be precise even if all are far from the true value.
Validity
whether the investigation measures what it set out to measure. It needs a fair test, where only the independent variable changes.
Results can be precise but not accurate, for example if a faulty balance gives the same wrong mass each time.
draft.remember: Accurate: near the true value. Precise: close together. Valid: measures the right thing.

a.q: Four titrations give volumes of 20.10, 20.12, 20.11 and 20.10 mL. The true value is 19.50 mL. How are these results best described?
opts: Precise but not accurate
Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
a.why: The results agree closely with each other, so they are precise. They are all about 0.6 mL from the true value, so they are not accurate. Accuracy depends on the true value, not on agreement.
a.clue: Compare the results with each other, then with the true value.

b.q: Jo tests how temperature affects dissolving by heating sugar in water. She also uses a larger amount of sugar in the hotter samples. Which statement is correct?
opts: Not valid, as more than one variable changed
Not precise, as the temperatures differ
Not accurate, as sugar was used
Valid, as the temperatures were measured
b.why: A valid test changes only the independent variable. Jo changed the amount of sugar as well, so she cannot tell which change affected dissolving. Measuring temperature does not fix that.
b.clue: Count how many things Jo changed between samples.

b.best: Not valid, as more than one variable changed

problems.detail: The clue 'Count how many things Jo changed between samples' points straight at the only option that mentions more than one variable changing. A student can pick it without understanding validity.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate and fit this point. The only issue is that the clue for question b nearly gives the answer away by telling students to count the variables Jo changed.
